The name Bartholomew means “son of Talmai” (or Tholmai). Fenlon (1907) notes that it may have been his own name, or a family name added to tell him apart.
No home given; Nathanael of Cana
There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples.
Scripture gives no home for Bartholomew. Nathanael was “of Cana in Galilee” (John 21:2).

Is Bartholomew the same man as Nathanael?
Its opening list of apostles names Bartholomew and Nathanael as two men. The same list also names Peter and Cephas as two.
Nathanael was not one of the Twelve
Augustine reasons that Nathanael “was learned and skilled in the law and for that reason was the Lord unwilling to place him among His disciples”, because he chose unlearned men.
The same man: Nathanael, son of Talmai
Ishodad of Merv (about 850); generally held from the 9th century on (Kerr, 1915); reasons set out by Fenlon (1907)

John never uses the name Bartholomew and the other Gospels never use Nathanael; the Gospel lists pair Bartholomew with Philip, who brought Nathanael; Nathanael was among disciples with apostles in John 21:2. Fenlon calls the case “ingenious and pretty strong”, with the weak link that Nathanael “may have been another personage”.
